Cadge

KAJ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To cadge is to beg for or get something by asking, especially persistently and for small things.

He was known around the dorm for cadging snacks from anyone with a full pantry.

Worked Example

Too broke to buy his own, he spent the whole party cadging cigarettes from anyone who'd give him one.

Going around a party begging cigarettes off anyone is exactly cadging.

Your Turn

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

mooch: To mooch is to freeload -- to live off other people's generosity without paying your way, often just taking what is offered rather than asking. To cadge is the more active habit: you ask outright, item by small item.

scrounge: To scrounge is to come up with things by hunting and foraging -- digging through bins, shelves, and leftovers for whatever can be found. To cadge is narrower: you get the thing from a person, by asking for it directly.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

provide: supply or give something needed

Where it sits · how habitual the one-sided taking is — borrow → cadge → sponge off

borrow vs. cadge: To borrow is milder than to cadge: borrowing carries an expected, often single, return of the item, while to cadge implies a habitual pattern of getting small things without giving anything back.

sponge off vs. cadge: To sponge off someone pushes the habit further than cadge, implying ongoing dependence on one source, while to cadge can describe a single small ask, like one pencil or one ride.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together

Put it together: Cadge is of uncertain origin, likely related to the dialect word cadger, a traveling peddler who went door to door -- a trade with a reputation for wheedling small favors along the way.

Use the root in a new word: cadger

Use the root in a new word: cadger: The related word cadger, an old dialect term for a traveling peddler, survives mostly in British regional speech and gives cadge its likely origin story.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Cadge is a casual, slightly disapproving word, almost always used for small, repeated asks -- a cigarette, a ride, a few dollars -- rather than one big favor.
